why_how.text: School buses use three light signals in sequence, and each one asks something different of you.
On a barrier-divided road, only traffic on the bus's side must stop for flashing red lights.

scenario.text: Jess is behind a school bus when its yellow overhead lights start flashing.

reasoning.text: Flashing yellow overhead lights mean get ready to stop, and flashing red overhead lights mean stop at least twenty feet back.

result.text: Jess slows and prepares to stop, then stops twenty feet back when the red lights come on.

claim.text: Common mistake: treating flashing yellow hazard lights on a bus the same as red overhead lights.

correction.text: Yellow hazard lights on a bus mean caution, yellow overhead lights mean prepare to stop, and only red overhead lights require you to stop twenty feet back.

prompt.text: A bus with flashing red overhead lights has stopped. When may you start moving again?

answer.text: When the red lights turn off or the bus moves on.

rationale.text: You stop at least twenty feet back and stay stopped until the red lights go off or the bus moves.

narration.text: This lesson is about reading the lights on a school bus. A bus can show flashing yellow hazard lights, flashing yellow overhead lights, or flashing red overhead lights, and each one tells you something different. Knowing which is which lets you react at the right moment instead of guessing. We will also look at what happens on a road divided by a barrier, where traffic going the other way may not have to stop. Practice questions usually describe one light and ask what you must do, so the goal is to connect each light to its action.

lines.text: Yellow overhead lights: get ready to stop.

narration.text: Flashing yellow hazard lights on a school bus mean proceed with caution. They do not require a stop. Flashing yellow overhead lights on a school bus mean get ready to stop. They warn you that the bus is about to stop and turn on its red lights. So the two yellow signals are different: hazard lights ask for caution, while the yellow overhead lights are the warning step before a stop. When you see yellow overhead lights, ease off the accelerator and prepare, so you are not forced into a sudden stop when the red lights begin.

lines.text: Red overhead: stop twenty feet back.
Stay until lights go off or bus moves.
Barrier: only the bus's side stops.

narration.text: Flashing red overhead lights mean stop at least twenty feet from the bus and stay stopped until the red lights turn off or the bus moves on. On a road divided by a barrier, oncoming vehicles need not stop for a school bus with flashing red lights, but vehicles on the bus's side of the road must stop. So the red lights always stop traffic behind the bus. Whether traffic in the other direction stops depends on the barrier. Without one, both directions stop. With a median or other barrier, only the bus's side does. Watch for the barrier.

lines.text: Trap: every flashing light means stop.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Yellow hazard lights on a bus mean caution, yellow overhead lights mean prepare to stop, and only red overhead lights require you to stop twenty feet back. Options may say that any flashing light on a bus means stop, or that yellow overhead lights require an immediate stop. Both are wrong. Another trap is leaving too soon. After the red lights come on, you stay stopped until they turn off or the bus moves on. Starting again as soon as the doors close, or after a few seconds, does not follow the rule.

lines.text: Bus stopped with red overhead lights.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a school bus has stopped with flashing red overhead lights, and you have stopped at least twenty feet behind it. When may you start moving again? Recall the red light rule. You stay stopped until the red lights turn off or the bus moves on. So the answer is not when the doors close or when you think the children are done crossing. It is when the red lights go off or the bus pulls away. Children may still be near the road, so start again carefully even then. Patience protects the children who may still be crossing.

To finish, flashing yellow hazard lights on a school bus mean proceed with caution, flashing yellow overhead lights mean get ready to stop, and flashing red overhead lights mean stop at least twenty feet from the bus and stay stopped until the red lights turn off or the bus moves on. On a road divided by a barrier, oncoming vehicles need not stop, but vehicles on the bus's side must stop. The hook to remember is caution, ready, stop: three lights, three actions, and only the red overhead lights require a full stop.

title.text: Yielding on turns and green lights

why_how.text: The turning driver yields: whether turning right, left, or on a red light, you yield to other vehicles.
A green light does not clear the intersection for you; vehicles still in it and oncoming traffic come first.

scenario.text: Leo waits on a two-way street to turn left on red onto a one-way street.

reasoning.text: Turning left on red from a two-way street onto a one-way street requires a full stop, a scan to the right, and yielding to opposite vehicles turning right.

result.text: Leo stops, scans right, yields to opposite vehicles turning right, then turns when clear.

claim.text: Many people think a green light means they may go no matter what is in the intersection.

correction.text: A green light does not give you the right of way over vehicles still clearing the intersection or over oncoming traffic when you turn left.

prompt.text: You are partway through a left turn on green when the signal turns red. What should you do?

answer.text: Finish the turn as quickly and safely as possible.

rationale.text: Once you are in the intersection waiting to turn, you complete the turn safely when the light turns red.

lines.text: Right turns, left turns, turns on red.
What green does and does not mean.

narration.text: This lesson covers yielding when you turn and when your light turns green. The basic idea is that the driver who is turning usually yields. That holds for right turns, left turns and turns on red. We will also cover the special steps for turning left on red between one-way and two-way streets, and what to do when your light has just turned green but the intersection is not yet clear. Many people believe a green light gives them full right of way. The handbook says otherwise, and practice questions often test exactly that belief.

lines.text: Turning right, including on red: yield.
Turning left from a driveway or alley: yield.
Finishing a left on green: yield.

narration.text: You must yield to other vehicles when turning right, including a right turn at a red light. You must yield to other vehicles when turning left, whether out of a driveway or alley or while finishing a left turn on a green light. A left turn on a red light also requires yielding to other vehicles. So in every one of these turning situations, other vehicles have the right of way and you wait for a safe gap. A turn on red is allowed only after you have yielded, never as a way to cut ahead of traffic that has the green.

lines.text: Look for traffic from your right.

narration.text: Before turning left on red from one one-way street onto another, stop completely and look for traffic coming from your right. This is one of the two situations where a left on red can be legal. The full stop comes first, then the look to the right, because traffic on the one-way street you are entering comes from that side. If a vehicle is approaching, you wait. You also still yield to pedestrians, as you will learn in the pedestrian lesson. A rolling left on red is never allowed, even on an empty one-way street. Never skip the stop.

lines.text: Yield to opposite vehicles turning right.

narration.text: Turning left on red from a two-way street onto a one-way street requires a full stop, a scan to the right, and yielding to opposite vehicles turning right. This adds one step to the one-way case. Because you are coming from a two-way street, vehicles facing you may also be turning right onto the same one-way street. They have the right of way over your left on red. So after your full stop, check to the right and watch the opposite side for right-turning vehicles. Only when both are clear may you make the turn. The extra yield is the key.

lines.text: Yield to vehicles still in the intersection.
Left on green after oncoming clears.
Light turns red mid-turn: finish safely.

narration.text: When your light has just turned green, yield to any vehicles still in the intersection before you go. On a green light, turn left only after all oncoming traffic has cleared, and if the light turns red while you are in the intersection, finish the turn as quickly and safely as possible. So green means you may go when it is safe, not that you may go immediately. Look for vehicles finishing their crossing and for oncoming traffic before you move. And if you are already in the intersection waiting to turn, you complete the turn rather than backing up.

lines.text: Yield to oncoming traffic on a left.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A green light does not give you the right of way over vehicles still clearing the intersection or over oncoming traffic when you turn left. Options may describe a driver who goes the instant the light turns green and then claim that driver was right. That is wrong if a vehicle was still in the intersection. Similarly, a driver turning left on green must wait for oncoming traffic, even though the light is green for both. Green tells you that you may proceed when the way is clear, and you still check before moving.

Here is a quick check: you are partway into the intersection waiting to turn left on a green light, and the light turns red before oncoming traffic clears. What should you do? Recall the left-on-green rule. You turn left only after oncoming traffic has cleared, and if the light turns red while you are in the intersection, you finish the turn as quickly and safely as possible. So you complete the turn once it is safe. You do not back out of the intersection and you do not sit through the next cycle blocking traffic.

lines.text: Left on red needs a full stop.

narration.text: To wrap up, you yield to other vehicles when turning right, including on red, and when turning left from a driveway, an alley, or on a green light, and also on a left turn on red. A left on red from one one-way street onto another needs a full stop and a look to the right; from a two-way street onto a one-way street, you also yield to opposite vehicles turning right. When your light turns green, yield to vehicles still in the intersection, and turn left only after oncoming traffic clears. Finish a turn safely if the light changes.

why_how.text: At four-way stops and broken signals, arrival order decides who goes, and ties go to the vehicle on the right.
Different signals ask for different actions: a flashing red needs a full stop, while a flashing yellow arrow needs only yielding.

scenario.text: Mia reaches a T-intersection on a road that ends, with no signs or signals, as a car approaches on the through road.

reasoning.text: At a T-intersection with no signals or signs, vehicles on the through road have the right of way.

result.text: Mia yields to the car on the through road before turning.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the driver on the left always yields at a four-way stop.

correction.text: At a four-way stop the first to stop goes first, and only on a tie does the driver on the left yield to the driver on the right.

prompt.text: The power is out and a signal is dark. Two cars reach it at the same moment. Who goes first?

answer.text: The car on the right goes first, after both have stopped completely.

rationale.text: A malfunctioning signal is treated like a stop: stop fully, let vehicles already there go, and on a tie yield to the right.

narration.text: This lesson covers how right of way works at intersections controlled by signs or by no signs at all. We will start with how to stop correctly at a stop sign or flashing red signal, then cover four-way stops, malfunctioning signals, flashing yellow arrows, T-intersections and YIELD signs. Each one has its own rule about who goes first and whether you must stop. Many questions here describe two vehicles arriving at once and ask who yields. The tie-breaking rule is the same in several cases, which makes it worth learning well.

lines.text: Use the stop line or crosswalk.
Otherwise, a spot with a clear view.

narration.text: At a stop sign or flashing red signal, stop completely and check traffic, using the stop line or crosswalk, or else a spot where you can see approaching traffic without entering the intersection. So the stop line comes first. If there is no line, stop before the crosswalk. If there is neither, stop where you can see cross traffic, but before you enter the intersection itself. A rolling stop is not a stop. Your wheels must come to a full stop, and only then do you check traffic and decide when it is safe to go. A full stop means zero motion.

lines.text: First to arrive and stop goes first.
Dark signal: treat like a stop.

narration.text: At a four-way stop, the first driver to arrive and stop goes first, and when two arrive together the vehicle on the left yields to the one on its right. At a malfunctioning traffic signal, stop completely, yield to vehicles already there, and yield to the vehicle on your right if you arrive together. So a dark or broken signal works the same way as a four-way stop. Arrival order decides first, and a tie goes to the vehicle on the right. Never treat a dark signal as a green light, even if the road looks empty. Learn the tie rule well.

lines.text: Flashing yellow arrow: yield, then turn.
T-intersection: through road has right of way.
YIELD sign: slow, check, be ready.

narration.text: At a flashing yellow arrow, yield to traffic before you complete your turn. At a T-intersection with no signals or signs, vehicles on the through road have the right of way. At a YIELD sign, slow down, check for traffic and be ready to stop. None of these requires a full stop every time, but each one requires you to give way when other traffic is present. The flashing yellow arrow lets you turn without a stop if the way is clear, and the YIELD sign lets you continue at a slower speed when no one is coming. Each sign asks you to give way.

Let us connect two signals that are easy to confuse. A flashing yellow arrow lets you turn but only after yielding, while a flashing red signal requires a complete stop first. Both flash, and both ask you to be careful, but the flashing red works like a stop sign. The flashing yellow arrow does not require a stop if no traffic is coming. Picture the color: red always means stop first, and yellow means yield. Then remember that after a flashing red stop, you still follow the same arrival and tie rules as at a stop sign.

lines.text: Ending road yields to through road.

narration.text: Here is the trap. At a four-way stop the first to stop goes first, and only on a tie does the driver on the left yield to the driver on the right. Options may say the left driver always yields, even if they arrived first. That is wrong. A malfunctioning signal is treated the same way: stop fully, let vehicles already there go, and on a tie yield to the right. Another trap is the T-intersection. At a T-intersection without signs, the driver on the ending road yields to traffic on the through road, whichever direction they come from.

Here is a quick check: the power is out, the traffic signal is dark, and two cars reach the intersection at the same moment from different directions. Who goes first? Recall how a malfunctioning signal is treated. It works like a stop. Both drivers stop completely, vehicles already at the intersection go first, and when two arrive together, each yields to the vehicle on its right. So the car on the right goes first. If you said whoever is faster or whoever is on the main road, remember that a dark signal falls back to the stop rules.

lines.text: Full stop at signs and flashing reds.
First stops, first goes; ties yield right.
Yield at arrows, T-intersections and YIELD signs.

narration.text: To finish, at a stop sign or flashing red signal, stop completely at the line, the crosswalk or a spot with a clear view, then check traffic. At a four-way stop or a malfunctioning signal, the first to stop goes first, and on a tie the vehicle on the left yields to the one on its right. At a flashing yellow arrow, yield before turning. At a T-intersection with no signs, the through road has the right of way. At a YIELD sign, slow down, check for traffic and be ready to stop. First stops, first goes. Ties always go to the right.

why_how.text: Workers and roadside service vehicles are exposed to traffic, so you should be ready to yield to them.
Funeral processions have strong right of way: you must not cut through one, though you need not pull over.
At a MERGE sign, through traffic has the right of way, so the merging driver adjusts speed and yields.

scenario.text: Nora meets a funeral procession with orange flags crossing an intersection ahead of her.

reasoning.text: A funeral procession has the right of way over all vehicles except fire trucks, ambulances and police vehicles, and cutting through one is a civil infraction.

result.text: Nora waits for the procession to pass instead of cutting through a gap.

claim.text: Myth: drivers must pull over and stop whenever they meet a funeral procession.

correction.text: Funeral processions outrank all traffic except fire, ambulance and police vehicles, yet you are not required to pull over for one; you only must not cut through it.

prompt.text: You reach a MERGE sign on an on-ramp. What should you do?

answer.text: Adjust your speed and yield to through traffic so you can merge safely.

rationale.text: At a MERGE sign, through traffic has the right of way, so you match your speed and fit in safely.

narration.text: This lesson covers right-of-way situations that do not involve a simple intersection. We will look at workers and stopped service vehicles, emergency vehicles approaching with lights and sirens, merging into through traffic, and funeral processions. Each situation has its own rule, and some of them surprise people. For example, many drivers think they must pull over for a funeral procession, but the rule is different. We will also connect the funeral procession rules to the emergency vehicles that still outrank a procession, so the order of priority is clear.

lines.text: Be ready to yield to workers.
Also to stopped service vehicles with flashing lights.

narration.text: Be ready to yield to workers in construction or maintenance areas and when nearing or passing a stopped garbage, utility or road maintenance vehicle with flashing lights. When an emergency vehicle approaches with red or blue lights and a siren, pull right next to the curb or edge, clear of any intersection, and stop until it passes or an officer waves you on. So for workers and service vehicles, you stay ready to give way. For an approaching emergency vehicle with a siren, you take a specific action: move right, stay out of intersections, and stop.

lines.text: At a MERGE sign, adjust your speed.

narration.text: At a MERGE sign, adjust your speed and yield to through traffic so you can merge safely. Through traffic has the right of way, so the merging driver is the one who adapts. Adjusting speed can mean speeding up to match traffic or slowing to fit into a gap. What you should not do is force your way in or stop suddenly at the end of a ramp unless you truly have no gap. The goal is a smooth merge that does not make through traffic brake hard. Check your mirrors and blind spot as you choose your gap. Smooth and steady is the goal.

lines.text: Right of way over all but fire, ambulance, police.
Orange flag with a religious symbol.
Cutting through is a civil infraction.

narration.text: A funeral procession has the right of way over all vehicles except fire trucks, ambulances and police vehicles. Procession vehicles must fly a fluorescent orange flag bearing a religious symbol such as a cross, a star of David, or a crescent and star. Cutting through a funeral procession is a civil infraction, though drivers are not required to pull over when they meet one. So you let the procession pass through intersections, you do not slip into gaps between its vehicles, and you are not required to stop on the shoulder as it goes by.

Here is the trap. Funeral processions outrank all traffic except fire, ambulance and police vehicles, yet you are not required to pull over for one; you only must not cut through it. Options may say you must pull over and stop, as you would for an emergency vehicle with a siren. That is not the rule for processions. A related trap is the ranking. A procession outranks ordinary traffic, but fire trucks, ambulances and police vehicles still outrank the procession. If an option says a procession has priority over an ambulance, it is wrong.

Here is a quick check: you are driving up an on-ramp toward a MERGE sign, and traffic is flowing steadily on the highway. What should you do? Recall the merge rule. At a MERGE sign, you adjust your speed and yield to through traffic so you can merge safely. So you match the speed of traffic and fit into a safe gap, giving way to vehicles already on the road. Through traffic is not required to make room for you. If you answered that the highway drivers must let you in, remember that the merging driver yields. Through traffic keeps the right of way.

lines.text: Yield to workers and service vehicles.

narration.text: To close, be ready to yield to workers in work areas and to stopped garbage, utility or road maintenance vehicles with flashing lights. For an emergency vehicle with lights and a siren, pull right to the curb or edge, clear of intersections, and stop until it passes or an officer waves you on. At a MERGE sign, adjust speed and yield to through traffic. A funeral procession, marked by orange flags with a religious symbol, outranks all vehicles except fire, ambulance and police vehicles. Do not cut through it, though you need not pull over.

why_how.text: Pedestrians in crosswalks have the right of way, and a green light never overrides one already crossing.
Turning drivers must watch for people on foot at every intersection, with or without signals.
Where no traffic control devices exist, a pedestrian in an unmarked crosswalk on the driver's half of the road gets the right of way.

scenario.text: Raj is waiting at a green light to turn right as a pedestrian steps off the curb into the crosswalk.

reasoning.text: You yield to pedestrians on every turn at an intersection, and to pedestrians in a marked crosswalk even when your light is green.

result.text: Raj waits for the pedestrian to cross before turning.

claim.text: Many people think a green light gives drivers priority over pedestrians in the crosswalk.

correction.text: A green light never overrides a pedestrian already in the crosswalk.

prompt.text: On a street with no signs or signals, a person starts across an unmarked crosswalk on your half of the road. Who has the right of way?

rationale.text: Where no traffic control devices exist, a pedestrian in an unmarked crosswalk on the driver's half of the road gets the right of way.

narration.text: This lesson covers when drivers must yield to pedestrians. Pedestrians are the most vulnerable people on the road, and the rules give them the right of way in many situations, including some where your light is green. We will go through marked crosswalks, school zones, turns at intersections, stops and flashing signals, unmarked crosswalks, and pedestrians who are already crossing. As you learn each rule, notice how often the answer is the same: yield. The skill is recognizing every situation where it applies, especially the ones where a green light might tempt you to go.

Yield to pedestrians in a marked crosswalk, whether at an intersection or midblock, even when your light is green. Yield to children in or near a school zone crosswalk while school is in session, and to pedestrians with physical, hearing or visual disabilities. Marked crosswalks are not only at corners. A midblock crosswalk gives pedestrians the same right of way. And in a school zone, children near the crosswalk count, not just those already in it. Pedestrians with disabilities may need more time, so you yield and give them that time.

lines.text: Yield on every turn at an intersection.
Yield at stops and flashing reds.

narration.text: Yield to pedestrians on every turn at an intersection, whether or not lights or traffic control devices are present. Yield to pedestrians when stopping at a stop sign or flashing red light and at an intersection with a flashing yellow light. So turning is a key moment. Whether you turn left or right, on a green, at a stop sign, or at an intersection with no signals at all, check for people crossing the street you are turning onto. A flashing yellow light lets traffic continue with caution, but pedestrians at that intersection still come first.

lines.text: Unmarked crosswalk on your half: pedestrian first.
Already in the crosswalk before the change.

narration.text: Where no traffic control devices exist, a pedestrian using an unmarked crosswalk on the driver's half of the road gets the right of way. Yield to a pedestrian who stepped into a crosswalk before the signal changed, and to one crossing from an alley, driveway, building or private road. An unmarked crosswalk is the natural crossing path at an intersection even without painted lines. And a pedestrian who started crossing legally does not lose the right of way when the light changes. They finish crossing first. The same care applies when you cross a sidewalk from a driveway.

lines.text: Marked crosswalks win even on green.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A green light never overrides a pedestrian already in the crosswalk. Options may describe a driver with a fresh green light who goes while someone is still crossing, and then claim the driver had the right of way. That is wrong. The same idea applies to marked crosswalks in general. You yield to pedestrians in a marked crosswalk at an intersection or midblock, even when your light is green. If the question includes a pedestrian in the crosswalk, the pedestrian almost always goes first, whatever color the light shows.

Here is a quick check: you are driving on a street with no signs or signals, and a person starts across an unmarked crosswalk on your half of the road. Who has the right of way? Recall the unmarked crosswalk rule. Where no traffic control devices exist, a pedestrian using an unmarked crosswalk on the driver's half of the road gets the right of way. So the pedestrian goes first, and you stop and wait for them to cross. The lack of painted lines does not take away the pedestrian's right of way at that crossing point.

To wrap up, yield to pedestrians in marked crosswalks, at intersections or midblock, even on a green light. Yield to children near school zone crosswalks during school, and to pedestrians with disabilities. Yield on every turn at an intersection, with or without signals, and at stop signs, flashing reds and flashing yellows. Where no devices exist, a pedestrian in an unmarked crosswalk on your half of the road has the right of way. Yield to people who started crossing before the light changed and to those crossing from alleys, driveways and buildings. Crosswalk beats green.

why_how.text: Passing needs time, distance and a clear view, so you pass only when oncoming traffic is far enough away.
Passing on the right is allowed only in listed cases and never by using the shoulder or leaving the road.
You must be back in your lane before coming within two hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle.

scenario.text: Ty is on a two-lane road behind a car that has stopped to turn left, with a wide paved lane beside it.

reasoning.text: You may pass on the right on a two-lane road with room when the vehicle ahead is turning left, but never by driving on the shoulder.

result.text: Ty passes on the right using the paved lane space, not the shoulder.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you may move back right as soon as your front bumper clears the car you passed.

correction.text: After passing, do not cut back right until the whole vehicle you passed shows in your rearview mirror.

prompt.text: While you are passing on a two-lane road, how close may you get to an oncoming vehicle before you are back in your lane?

answer.text: You must be back in your lane before you come within two hundred feet of it.

rationale.text: The return rule is two hundred feet from oncoming traffic, which is why you need a clear view and enough distance before you pass.

narration.text: This lesson covers how to pass another vehicle safely. Passing on a two-lane road means driving in the lane used by oncoming traffic, which makes it one of the riskiest moves in everyday driving. We will cover when you may pass, how to return to your lane, the distance you must keep from oncoming traffic, extra care for trailers and three-lane roads, what to do when someone passes you, and the limited cases when you may pass on the right. The next lesson then covers the situations where passing is banned altogether.

lines.text: Clear view of the left lane.
Return when the car shows in your mirror.

narration.text: On a two-lane highway, pass only with a clear view of the left lane and oncoming traffic far enough away to give you the time and distance to pass safely. After passing, do not cut back right until the whole vehicle you passed shows in your rearview mirror. You must be back in your lane before coming within two hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle. Those three rules work together. The clear view lets you judge the distance, the mirror check keeps you from cutting off the car you passed, and the two hundred feet keeps you safe from oncoming traffic.

lines.text: Pass one vehicle at a time.

narration.text: Allow extra passing room when towing a trailer, pass only one vehicle at a time, and do not tailgate a vehicle that is passing slower traffic. Use extreme care when passing in the center lane of a three-lane road, since oncoming drivers may enter it too, and never use it to pass or merge when it is marked for left turns only. A trailer makes your vehicle longer, so a pass takes more distance. Passing several cars at once keeps you in the oncoming lane too long. And the center lane of a three-lane road may be shared with drivers coming the other way.

When someone is passing you, do not speed up or race them; let them finish safely. A driver who is passing is exposed in the oncoming lane, and speeding up makes the pass longer and more dangerous for everyone. Keep a steady speed, or ease off slightly if that helps them return to the lane. Racing a passer can trap them beside you as oncoming traffic approaches. The safest choice is to let the pass happen quickly. Your role here is simple: hold your lane, hold your speed, and do not compete. Steady speed helps the passer finish.

lines.text: Left turner ahead, or extra lanes.

narration.text: Passing on the right is allowed in limited cases but never by driving on the shoulder or off the road. You may pass on the right on a two-lane road with room when the vehicle ahead is turning left, on a multi-lane one-way street, on roads with two or more lanes each way, or where the road is widened for passing. So the list is specific. Outside those cases, pass on the left. And even in those cases, you stay on the pavement. Using the shoulder to get around a car is not passing on the right legally. Outside those cases, pass on the left.

lines.text: Trap: shoulder is fine if paved.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Passing on the right is legal in the listed cases, but using the shoulder or leaving the pavement to do it never is. Options may describe a driver using a paved shoulder to get around a left-turning car and call it legal. It is not. The left-turner case allows passing on the right only when there is room on the road itself. A second trap is the return to your lane. You may not cut back as soon as you clear the other car. You wait until the whole vehicle you passed shows in your rearview mirror. Stay on the pavement.

Here is a quick check: you are passing on a two-lane road and see an oncoming vehicle ahead. How close may you get to it before you must be back in your own lane? Recall the return rule. You must be back in your lane before coming within two hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle. That is why you only start a pass when you have a clear view and oncoming traffic is far enough away to give you the time and distance. If you are not sure you can finish the pass before two hundred feet, do not start it. When in doubt, wait for a better chance.

lines.text: Back by two hundred feet; mirror check.
Right-side passing only in listed cases.

narration.text: To close, pass on a two-lane highway only with a clear view and oncoming traffic far enough away. Be back in your lane before two hundred feet from an oncoming vehicle, and return only when the whole vehicle you passed shows in your rearview mirror. Allow extra room when towing, pass one vehicle at a time, and do not tailgate a passer. Use extreme care in a three-lane center lane. When you are passed, do not speed up. Pass on the right only in the listed cases, and never on the shoulder. See it in the mirror. Patience makes passing safe.

why_how.text: Passing is banned where you cannot see far enough or where traffic may cross your path, such as hills, curves, intersections and railroad crossings.
You may not pass vehicles stopped for pedestrians or a school bus with red lights flashing.

scenario.text: Ana approaches a railroad crossing about eighty feet ahead and the slow car in front is tempting her to pass.

reasoning.text: Do not pass within one hundred feet of an intersection or railroad crossing.

result.text: Ana stays behind the slow car until she is past the crossing and has a safe, legal place to pass.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the center lane of a three-lane road is always open for passing.

correction.text: The center lane of a three-lane road may be used to pass unless it is marked for left turns only, in which case passing and merging there are banned.

prompt.text: Which two distances matter when passing: the one for oncoming traffic and the one for intersections and railroad crossings?

answer.text: Be back in your lane before two hundred feet from oncoming traffic, and do not pass within one hundred feet of an intersection or railroad crossing.

rationale.text: The two hundred foot rule protects you from oncoming vehicles, while the one hundred foot rule keeps you from passing near crossings.

narration.text: This lesson covers the situations where passing is banned. Some bans come from markings and signs on the road. Others come from limited visibility, like hills and curves. Others involve places where traffic or pedestrians may cross your path, like intersections and railroad crossings, and there are bans tied to stopped vehicles and school buses. Practice questions often present a tempting pass and ask whether it is allowed, so it helps to have a mental checklist of every banned situation. We will also compare two distances that people tend to confuse.

lines.text: Solid yellow line on your side.

narration.text: Passing is banned when your side of the center has a solid yellow line, when no-passing signs are posted, or when a hill or curve hides oncoming traffic. Do not pass when oncoming traffic is too close, when you cannot see clearly ahead, or when the three-lane center lane is marked left turn only. These rules share one idea: you need to see far enough ahead to know the pass is safe. A solid yellow line on your side tells you the road designers decided you cannot. And a hill or curve can hide an oncoming car until it is too late.

lines.text: Not within one hundred feet of an intersection.
Or where a bridge or tunnel blocks your view.

narration.text: Do not pass within one hundred feet of an intersection or railroad crossing, or when a bridge, viaduct or tunnel within one hundred feet blocks your view. Intersections and crossings are places where other traffic, trains or pedestrians may enter your path, and passing there leaves you in the wrong lane at the worst moment. Bridges, viaducts and tunnels can hide what is coming. So one hundred feet is the distance to watch near these places. If a crossing or intersection is that close, stay in your lane and wait until you are well past it.

lines.text: School bus with red lights flashing.

narration.text: Do not pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk or intersection for a pedestrian, in a posted no-passing construction zone, or when a school bus has stopped with red lights flashing. A stopped car at a crosswalk may be hiding a pedestrian you cannot see, so going around it is especially dangerous. Construction zones may post no-passing rules because workers and equipment are close to the lanes. And a stopped school bus with flashing red lights requires you to stop, not to pass. In all three cases, the stopped vehicle is a signal to stop or wait.

title.text: Two distances and the center lane

narration.text: Here is the trap. After passing, you must be back in your lane before you are within two hundred feet of oncoming traffic, while the no-passing distance near intersections and railroad crossings is one hundred feet. Options may use one number for both. A second trap is the three-lane center lane. It may be used to pass unless it is marked for left turns only, in which case passing and merging there are banned. So check the markings: a turn-only center lane is never a passing lane, even if it is empty at the moment.

Here is a quick check: two distances matter when passing. What is the distance for oncoming traffic, and what is the distance for intersections and railroad crossings? Recall both rules. You must be back in your lane before coming within two hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle. And you must not pass within one hundred feet of an intersection or railroad crossing. So the answers are two hundred feet for oncoming traffic and one hundred feet for crossings. If you swapped them, picture the oncoming car needing more room because both vehicles are moving toward each other.

lines.text: Not within one hundred feet of crossings.
Never pass a stopped bus or crosswalk stop.

narration.text: To finish, passing is banned with a solid yellow line on your side, at posted no-passing signs, when a hill or curve hides oncoming traffic, when oncoming traffic is too close, when you cannot see clearly ahead, and in a three-lane center lane marked left turn only. Do not pass within one hundred feet of an intersection or railroad crossing, or near a bridge, viaduct or tunnel that blocks your view. Do not pass a vehicle stopped for a pedestrian, in a posted no-passing work zone, or a school bus stopped with red lights flashing.
